rationale: A wins because it keeps four real stories inside the fence of the supplied facts. A's "Allbirds adds a wholesale partner as it pulls back from its own stores" is a clean channel angle; B's "A DTC pioneer that spent a decade avoiding wholesale" takes the same fact and smuggles in company history the update did not give. B has sharper teeth in places, but teeth attached to invented claims still get knocked out by a reporter with notes open.
gaps_in_A: "Story type: funding-mechanics" mislabels an earnings/turnaround angle; this is public-company retail performance, not funding mechanics.

"The prevailing belief in DTC retail is that growth comes from expanding the range and the store footprint" is plausible but unsupported by the supplied update. Bring evidence or phrase it as a question.
"a brand that built itself on direct retail is leaning on someone else's shelves" imports DTC origin-story context not provided in the facts. The channel tension works without that decoration.

The materials angle stops at durability testing and leaves the sustainability-performance question underdeveloped; that may be a live angle if Allbirds can prove longevity changes the environmental claim.
gaps_in_B: "That's a company publicly conceding its signature product had a durability problem" overstates the fact. "More durable than the original" is not a confession that the original failed.
"A DTC pioneer that spent a decade avoiding wholesale" is invented from thin air. The update says there is a wholesale partnership, not a decade-long anti-wholesale history.
"the collapse of the direct-to-consumer orthodoxy and the return of brands to third-party shelves" is a big trend frame with no supplied evidence. Good phrase, bad discipline.

"natural, low-carbon materials" and "a shoe replaced twice as often is worse regardless of its carbon footprint" drag in carbon and lifecycle claims the update did not provide. That may become a story after proof; right now it is a thesis wearing a borrowed coat.
